tool.name: VRM
tool.summary: Computes the Vector Ruggedness Measure (VRM), a topographic roughness index (Sappington et al. 2007) that quantifies the 3D dispersion of unit vectors orthogonal to the terrain surface within a neighborhood of each cell -- the spherical analog of circular variance (Fisher 1993). Distinguishes steep-but-even terrain from steep, broken terrain; correct on geographic (latitude/longitude) DEMs.
tool.usage:
Most measures of terrain ruggedness -- contour density, sums of elevation differences -- are strongly correlated with slope: a steep, smooth hillside scores as "rugged" even though it is perfectly even. VRM (Sappington, Longshore, and Thompson 2007, developed for bighorn sheep habitat analysis) avoids this by measuring how much the orientation of the terrain surface varies within a neighborhood, independent of how steep it is on average. Every cell has a unit vector orthogonal (normal) to its local surface, pointing straight up from a flat cell and increasingly sideways as the cell steepens. On a smooth slope, neighboring cells' normal vectors all point in nearly the same direction; on broken, uneven terrain, they scatter in many directions even if the average steepness is identical.
VRM measures this scatter directly: it sums the normal vectors of every cell in a neighborhood as if they were unit steps strung end to end (vector addition), takes the length of that resultant, and divides by the number of vectors -- the mean resultant length, exactly the statistic Fisher (1993, eq. 2.10) defines for circular data, generalized here from the circle to the sphere. A value near 1 means the vectors nearly canceled out (widely scattered, high ruggedness); a value near 0 means they reinforced each other (all pointing the same way). VRM is reported as 1 minus this quantity -- Fisher's circular variance (eq. 2.11) -- so it reads like other ruggedness indices: 0 for a flat or uniformly sloped neighborhood, up to 1 for maximum dispersion. A steep but even slope scores near 0, just like flat ground; only terrain that is both steep and broken scores high.
The neighborhood is circular, with a radius you choose in cells or ground units (meters, kilometers, feet, or miles; ground-unit radii are converted to cells geodesically, per row, on geographic DEMs, matching the Blurred Hillshade tool's radius convention). Because a diagonal neighbor sits sqrt(2) cells away, the smallest radius that reproduces Sappington's original 3 x 3 neighborhood (all 8 surrounding cells plus the focal cell) is 1.5 cells -- the default; a radius of exactly 1 cell gives a smaller 5-cell "plus" neighborhood (the 4 orthogonal neighbors only). Larger radii examine ruggedness at a coarser landscape scale; there is no fixed relationship between radius and the resulting VRM values (a larger window can capture more terrain diversity, not less), so experiment with a few radii to find the scale relevant to your question.
Computing each cell's own orthogonal vector requires its full 3 x 3 neighborhood, so elevation data is read out to your chosen radius plus one additional cell -- you do not need to buffer the input yourself. The neighborhood aggregation ignores NoData: VRM is computed wherever at least one valid orthogonal vector falls within the radius, even where the focal cell's own elevation is NoData (the same gap-filling behavior as the Blurred Hillshade tool); cells with no valid neighbor vector at all are NoData in the output.
Optional local detrending (Dilts et al. 2023). Even though VRM is independent of average slope, it can still be inflated on smooth folds -- ridgelines and drainages read as rugged simply because adjacent cells face different directions, even where the surface itself is smooth. Turning on "Remove smooth topography first" subtracts a circular neighborhood mean of the DEM (the smoothing radius you set, default 1.5 cells = a 3 x 3 mean) before VRM is computed, leaving only the fine-scale surface variation. The result is what Dilts et al. (2023) call the "local" variant (VRM-L): it measures surface roughness in its own right and passes all three of their "ideal ruggedness" criteria -- independent of slope, unaffected by smooth folding, and rising only with true vertical roughness. The detrending neighborhood is separate from, and usually smaller than, the VRM radius. Dilts et al. describe three "generations" of ruggedness index: first-generation indices (elevation variability, e.g. the surface ratio or TRI) are correlated with slope; second-generation indices (VRM, and the Arc-Chord Ratio) remove the slope correlation but are still fooled by smooth folds; the third generation is exactly this local (detrended) family, which isolates fine-scale surface roughness.
Unlike a planar calculation, this tool is accurate for DEMs in geographic coordinate systems: surface gradients are computed from true spheroidal distances at every row's latitude. Elevation units are read from the DEM's vertical coordinate system when one is defined (geographic DEMs are assumed to be in meters); otherwise the tool asks you to choose meters or feet. The output is floating point (0 to 1) and carries statistics and a histogram so it renders correctly without a separate Calculate Statistics step; pyramids are built with bilinear resampling. This tool requires reading the whole DEM into memory at once.
References: Sappington, J. M., K. M. Longshore, and D. B. Thompson. 2007. Quantifying landscape ruggedness for animal habitat analysis: a case study using bighorn sheep in the Mojave Desert. Journal of Wildlife Management 71(5):1419-1426. The underlying statistic follows Hobson, R. D. 1972 (surface roughness in geomorphology) and Fisher, N. I. 1993. Statistical Analysis of Circular Data. Cambridge University Press (section 2.3, eq. 2.10-2.11). The unit orthogonal (normal) vector at each cell is derived from Horn's gradient: Horn, B. K. P. 1981. Hill shading and the reflectance map. Proceedings of the IEEE 69:14-47. The optional local detrending follows Dilts, T. E., M. E. Blum, K. T. Shoemaker, P. J. Weisberg, and K. M. Stewart. 2023. Improved topographic ruggedness indices more accurately model fine-scale ecological patterns. Landscape Ecology 38:1395-1410 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10980-023-01646-6).

dialogReference.para: The elevation raster (DEM) to compute VRM from. It must be single band. Choose a raster from the map or browse to one on disk.
The output VRM raster (floating point, 0 to 1; NoData where no valid orthogonal vector falls within the neighborhood). A suggested name is filled in from the input.

The DEM's elevation units, Meters or Feet. Filled in and locked automatically when the DEM defines a vertical coordinate system; geographic DEMs are assumed to be in meters. You are only asked to choose when the DEM does not say.

How far the neighborhood extends around each cell, in the radius units below. The default, 1.5 cells, reproduces Sappington's original 3 x 3 neighborhood (all 8 surrounding cells plus the focal cell). Larger values examine ruggedness at a coarser scale; experiment with a few radii to find the scale relevant to your question.

The units of the radius. Cells applies the same radius everywhere. Meters, Kilometers, Feet, and Miles are converted to cells from the raster's cell size - planarly for projected rasters, and per row on the spheroid (geodesic) for geographic rasters, so the neighborhood stays true at any latitude.

Turn on to locally detrend the DEM before computing VRM (Dilts et al. 2023): a circular neighborhood mean is subtracted from the DEM, leaving only the fine-scale surface variation, so smooth ridgelines and drainages no longer read as rugged. The result is Dilts's "local" variant, VRM-L. Off by default (the standard VRM).

The radius of the circular neighborhood mean used to smooth the DEM for detrending. The default, 1.5 cells, is exactly a 3 x 3 mean (the smoothing Dilts et al. 2023 used); larger radii remove broader-scale topography before the roughness is measured. Only used when detrending is on.

Units for the smoothing (detrending) radius: Cells, or a ground unit (Meters, Kilometers, Feet, Miles) converted to cells from the cell size - planarly for projected rasters, geodesically per row for geographic rasters. Only used when detrending is on.

scriptExample.title: VRM example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: VRM at the classic 3x3 scale, then the local (detrended) variant VRM-L with a 3x3 smoothing window. Valid detrend_units match the neighborhood units: "Cells", "Meters", "Kilometers", "Feet", "Miles".
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages arcpy.jenness.VRM( in_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM", out_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM_VRM_3x3", elev_units="Meters", radius=1.5, radius_units="Cells") arcpy.jenness.VRM( in_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM", out_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM_VRML", elev_units="Meters", radius=1.5, radius_units="Cells", detrend=True, detrend_radius=1.5, detrend_units="Cells")

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Vector Ruggedness Measure: topographic roughness from the 3D dispersion of unit vectors orthogonal to the terrain surface (Sappington et al. 2007), independent of slope, with correct geodesic handling of geographic DEMs.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Computes the Vector Ruggedness Measure (VRM) from a single-band DEM: unit vectors orthogonal to the terrain surface are summed by vector addition over a circular neighborhood of each cell (radius in cells or ground units, geodesic per row on geographic DEMs), and VRM is reported as 1 minus the standardized resultant length (Fisher 1993 circular variance, generalized to the sphere) - 0 for flat or uniformly sloped terrain, up to 1 for maximally dispersed, broken terrain, independent of average slope. Elevation data is read one cell beyond the chosen radius so every neighbor's own orthogonal vector can be computed; the aggregation ignores NoData. The output is floating point (0-1) and carries statistics and a histogram. References: Sappington, J. M., K. M. Longshore, and D. B. Thompson. 2007. Journal of Wildlife Management 71(5):1419-1426; Fisher, N. I. 1993. Statistical Analysis of Circular Data, Cambridge University Press.
